910.name: Dacians & Roman Dacia
910.description: The Dacian civilisation, centred in the Carpathian Mountains, rivalled Rome under King Decebalus. Trajan's conquest (101–106 CE) created the province of Dacia, whose romanisation became the foundation of Romanian identity and the Latin-derived Romanian language.

sub_clusters.name: Dacian Kingdoms
sub_clusters.description: The Getae-Dacian civilisation, King Burebista's unification of Dacian tribes (82–44 BCE), the mountain fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains (UNESCO), and King Decebalus's resistance to Roman expansion culminating in the Dacian Wars (101–106 CE).
key_events: Trajan's Dacian Wars (101–106 CE) — conquest and provincialization

sub_clusters.name: Roman Dacia & Romanisation
sub_clusters.description: The province of Dacia: Roman colonists, mines (Roșia Montană gold), urban centres (Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, Apulum), and the romanisation that produced the Romanian language. Emperor Aurelian's withdrawal (271 CE) and the Daco-Roman continuity debate.

920.name: Migration Period & Vlach Emergence
920.description: After the Roman withdrawal, successive migratory waves (Goths, Huns, Slavs, Avars, Bulgars, Magyars, Cumans) crossed the territory. The Romanised population (Vlachs) survived in mountain regions, gradually emerging as a distinct ethnic group.

sub_clusters.name: Barbarian Migrations & Slavic Influence
sub_clusters.description: Gothic, Hunnic, Avar, and Slavic migrations through the Carpathian-Danubian region. Slavic settlement influenced the Romanian language (40% of vocabulary) and Orthodox Christianity. The First and Second Bulgarian Empires extended influence over parts of the territory.

sub_clusters.name: Hungarian & Cuman Influence
sub_clusters.description: Magyar conquest of Transylvania (10th century), the Teutonic Knights' brief presence in Burzenland, Cuman and Pecheneg peoples south of the Carpathians, and the first recorded Vlach political formations.

920.name: Principalities of Wallachia & Moldavia
920.description: The founding of the principalities of Wallachia (c. 1290, Basarab I) and Moldavia (1359, Bogdan I) created the two pillars of Romanian statehood. Mircea the Elder and Stephen the Great defended their lands against Ottoman expansion.

sub_clusters.name: Founding of Wallachia & Mircea the Elder
sub_clusters.description: Basarab I's defeat of the Hungarian king at Posada (1330) secured Wallachian independence. Mircea the Elder (r. 1386–1418) expanded the principality and fought the Ottomans at Rovine (1395) and Nicopolis (1396).

sub_clusters.name: Vlad the Impaler & Stephen the Great
sub_clusters.description: Vlad III Dracula ('the Impaler', r. 1448/1456–1462/1476) — whose fierce resistance to the Ottomans inspired the Dracula legend — and Stephen the Great of Moldavia (r. 1457–1504), who won 36 of 38 battles and built 40 monasteries.
key_events: Vlad the Impaler's Night Attack on Mehmed II (June 17, 1462)
Stephen the Great's victory at Vaslui (1475)

930.name: Ottoman Suzerainty & Phanariot Era
930.description: Wallachia and Moldavia became Ottoman vassal states, retaining internal autonomy but paying heavy tribute. Michael the Brave briefly united all three Romanian lands (1600). The Phanariot era (1711–1821) saw Greek-origin princes governing under Ottoman direction.

sub_clusters.name: Michael the Brave & First Romanian Union
sub_clusters.description: Michael the Brave (Mihai Viteazul) briefly united Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania (1600) — a foundational moment in Romanian national mythology. His assassination (1601) ended the union, but it inspired later unification movements.
key_events: Michael the Brave unites Wallachia, Moldavia & Transylvania (1600)

sub_clusters.name: Phanariot Period & Decline
sub_clusters.description: Ottoman control tightened through appointed Phanariot Greek princes (1711 in Moldavia, 1716 in Wallachia). Fiscal exploitation, boyar resistance, and the Phanariots' paradoxical role in transmitting Enlightenment ideas. Tudor Vladimirescu's 1821 uprising ended Phanariot rule.

940.name: National Awakening & Unification
940.description: The Transylvanian School's assertion of Roman Dacian continuity, the 1848 Wallachian revolution, the union of Wallachia and Moldavia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza (1859), and Romanian independence won in the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78).

sub_clusters.name: 1848 Revolution & Reform
sub_clusters.description: Tudor Vladimirescu's 1821 uprising, the Transylvanian School's scholarly nationalism, the Organic Statutes (1831/1832), and the Wallachian revolution of 1848 — suppressed by joint Ottoman-Russian intervention — demanding modernisation and union.

sub_clusters.name: Union of Principalities & Independence
sub_clusters.description: Alexandru Ioan Cuza elected prince of both Moldavia and Wallachia (1859), creating the United Principalities (later Romania). Cuza's modernising reforms (land reform, secularisation), his replacement by Carol I (1866), and Romanian independence in the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78).
key_events: Union of Wallachia and Moldavia under Cuza (January 24, 1859)

940.name: Kingdom of Romania & Belle Époque
940.description: King Carol I proclaimed the Kingdom of Romania (1881). Rapid modernisation, the Bucharest Belle Époque, the peasant revolt of 1907, Romania's entry into WWI (1916), and the creation of Greater Romania (1918) uniting Transylvania, Bukovina, and Bessarabia.

sub_clusters.name: Kingdom & Modernisation
sub_clusters.description: Carol I's kingdom, the Bucharest Belle Époque, oil industry development (Romania as Europe's leading oil producer), the 1907 peasant revolt (11,000 killed), and the Balkan Wars (1912–13).

sub_clusters.name: WWI & Greater Romania
sub_clusters.description: Romania's entry into WWI (August 1916), initial defeats and the loss of Bucharest, the victories at Mărășești (1917), and the post-war unification creating Greater Romania (December 1, 1918 — Transylvania, plus Bukovina and Bessarabia), doubling the country's size.
key_events: Greater Romania proclaimed — union with Transylvania (December 1, 1918)

950.name: Interwar Romania & WWII
950.description: Greater Romania faced the rise of the fascist Iron Guard, King Carol II's royal dictatorship, territorial losses (1940), alliance with Nazi Germany, the switch of sides (August 1944), and participation in the liberation of Transylvania.

sub_clusters.name: Interwar Period & Iron Guard
sub_clusters.description: Greater Romania's democratic experiment, the rise of Corneliu Zelea Codreanu's fascist Iron Guard (Legion of the Archangel Michael), King Carol II's personal dictatorship (1938), and the catastrophic territorial losses of 1940 (Bessarabia, Northern Transylvania, Southern Dobruja).

sub_clusters.name: WWII & Switch of Sides
sub_clusters.description: Ion Antonescu's military dictatorship, alliance with Nazi Germany, the Holocaust in Romania (Iași pogrom, Transnistria deportations — 280,000–380,000 Jews and Roma killed), and King Michael's coup (August 23, 1944) switching Romania to the Allied side.
key_events: King Michael's Coup — Romania switches sides (August 23, 1944)

950.name: Communist Romania & Ceaușescu Regime
950.description: Soviet-imposed communism, Gheorghiu-Dej's Stalinist era, and Ceaușescu's increasingly megalomaniacal dictatorship — from initial independence from Moscow to bizarre personality cult, systematisation, and the destruction of Bucharest's historic centre.

sub_clusters.name: Soviet Occupation & Stalinism
sub_clusters.description: Forced abdication of King Michael (1947), communist takeover, Gheorghiu-Dej's Stalinist era, political terror, collectivisation, the Danube-Black Sea Canal (built with political prisoner labour), and Romania's assertion of independence from the Soviet Union.

sub_clusters.name: Ceaușescu Era
sub_clusters.description: Nicolae Ceaușescu's initial Western-leaning independence (denouncing 1968 Prague invasion), his descent into megalomaniacal dictatorship, personality cult, the 'systematisation' programme destroying villages, the Palace of the Parliament (world's heaviest building), and the economic austerity of the 1980s that impoverished the population.

960.name: 1989 Revolution & Democratic Romania
960.description: The Romanian Revolution of December 1989 — the only violent overthrow of a communist regime in Eastern Europe — executed Ceaușescu. Post-revolutionary Romania underwent a painful transition to democracy and market economy, culminating in EU accession (2007).

sub_clusters.name: 1989 Revolution & Transition
sub_clusters.description: The Romanian Revolution began in Timișoara (December 16, 1989), spread to Bucharest, and ended with the execution of Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu (December 25, 1989). Ion Iliescu's controversial presidency, the Mineriad violence, and the slow democratic and economic transition.
key_events: Romanian Revolution — Ceaușescu overthrown and executed (December 1989)

sub_clusters.name: EU Accession & Contemporary Romania
sub_clusters.description: NATO membership (2004), EU accession (January 1, 2007), ongoing anti-corruption struggles (DNA), massive diaspora emigration, the Colectiv nightclub fire (2015) sparking anti-corruption protests, and Romania's growing strategic importance in the context of the Ukraine war.
